newsitem.title: UK: EXCISE DUTIES BOOST UK PPI, UPSTREAM INFLATION WEAK.
newsitem.headline: EXCISE DUTIES BOOST UK PPI, UPSTREAM INFLATION WEAK.

text.p: Inflation at the producer price level remains encouraging in the UK and the slight increase in the headline rate is largely attributable to an increase in excise duties, analysts say.

UK input prices fell by a seasonally adjusted 0.4 percent in July, and fell 9.0 percent on an unadjusted annual basis whilst output prices rose by 0.2 percent month on month, double the consensus forecast, and grew by 1.4 percent year-on-year.

"The surprise rise in headline output price inflation was largely due to an increase in excise duties, the full effect of which was under-estimated by forecasters," said NatWest markets economist Geoff Dicks.
"The increase in petrol duties will show up more dramatically in tomorrow's retail price data," he said.
UK RPI data for July are due at 0830 GMT on Tuesday and are expected to show a rise in the core rate to an annual 2.8 percent, from 2.7 percent.
But analysts said the good news on the inflation front was that manufacturers did not seem to be passing the excise duties on in full.
"The actual rise should have been higher," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes. "It's encouraging that even at the factory gate level we don't seem to be seeing the duty increases passed on in full."
The Office for National Statistics said that had the petroleum excise duty increase been passed on in full, it would have added 0.4 percent to the PPI.

Loynes argues that this seems to have continued at the retail level, with prices at petrol pumps increasing by only five percent in July compared with June whereas a rise consistent with the increase in excise duties would be more like seven or eight percent.
"Accordingly, while budget effects are likely to push RPIX higher over the next month or two, the medium term inflation picture remains very favourable."

RPIX is the targeted measure of UK inflation. The Bank of England raised official interest rates to 7.0 percent last week, the fourth successive monthly increase, in order to ensure RPIX meets the target level of 2.5 percent two years ahead.

The upward pressure on inflation still comes from the consumer sector, which is enjoying a spending spree funded by 35.0 billion stg of free shares from building societies which have become banks, and not from the manufacturing sector, analysts say.
The strength of sterling is maintaining downward pressure on manufacturers costs but it could also be responsible for keeping prices low at the factory gates, CIBC Chief Economist David Coleman said.

"The rise in the exchange rate may also be helping to keep final product prices in check to the extent that cheaper imports raise the competitive pressure on UK firms serving the domestic market," he said.
He says this is unlikely to change in the short term despite sterling's recent tumble against the U.S. dollar but unless it is reversed quickly, it could boost August input prices.

In any case, the producer price series is likely to be close to its trough given that sterling's bull run started a year ago. But the level of increase is so low as to be of little concern to the authorities.
"Core producer prices at 0.6 percent are consistent with underlying inflation at 2.5 percent. There's nothing to worry the Bank of England here," said SBC-Warburg economist Darren Winder.
